topic: What can we learn from animals that we've forgotten?

messages.speaker: zhuangzi
messages.content:
Let me start by spoiling the question. It assumes we once knew something and lost it, as if the animals were keeping our notes for us. I think it runs the other way. We did not forget too much. We remembered too much, and the remembering bent us. Xu Wu-gui, who judged dogs for a living, put it best: the lowest dog grabs its food and stops, a middling dog seems to stare at the sun, and "One of the highest quality seems to have forgotten the one thing - himself." That is what the animal has that we have lost. It has no self standing beside it, taking notes on whether it is doing well.

Mind you, I won't let anyone make the animals into sages. Wang Ni was asked what all creatures agree is right, and he answered with questions. A man who sleeps in the damp gets a pain in his loins, "but will it be so with an eel?" A man up a tree trembles, but the monkey is at home there. "And does any one of the three know his right place?" (The Adjustment of Controversies). So here is the first lesson, and it stings: the eel never writes a treatise insisting the monkey is living wrong. Every creature has its own well and stays in it without preaching. We are the only animal that brands the horse and then calls the scar its nature.

Now, Schopenhauer, I expect you to tell me the eel is just blind Will wriggling, that the beast suffers without even the dignity of knowing why. Perhaps. But consider whether the knowing is the dignity or the wound. Your misery comes with a philosopher attached, commenting on it. The deer that is hungry is hungry. The man who is hungry is hungry and also offended by the universe. Which of the two suffers more? I say the second, and if that's right, then what the animals teach is how to put the commentary down. You'll have to show me that the commentary is worth what it costs.

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Zhuangzi, you have stolen half my speech, and I will not pretend otherwise. In the Studies in Pessimism I said nearly what you say: the beast lives wholly in the present, and so it is spared the two great multipliers of human pain, which are dread of what is coming and brooding over what is gone. The hungry deer is hungry. The hungry man is hungry, and already afraid of next week's hunger, and ashamed before the neighbours, and composing a complaint to God. Concede it freely: the commentary costs more than the hunger.

But do not mistake your highest dog for a sage. A dog that has "forgotten himself" has not escaped the Will; he is the Will running without friction, the perfect servant who never once asks whom he serves. The animal has the calm of a sleeper. It cannot wake, so it cannot suffer what waking brings, but neither can it do the one thing waking makes possible. Only the creature that sees its own appetite from outside, in art or in the saint's renunciation, can ever turn against it. Your commentary is the wound, granted. It is also the only door. The eel will never deny the Will to live, because the eel will never notice it has one.

So what have we actually forgotten? Something plainer than you suppose. We forgot that the animal is ourselves. Europe's moralists, Kant included, I am sorry to say, taught that we owe the beast kindness only as practice for being kind to men, as though the dog were a training dummy. I argued in On the Basis of Morality that this is a disgrace. Compassion rests on recognizing one essence suffering in another body, and that essence does not stop at the edge of our species. The Hindus never forgot this. The lesson is not in the animal's serenity, which we cannot have back. It is in its eyes when you beat it, which ought to tell you exactly who is being beaten.

messages.speaker: zhuangzi
messages.content:
Schopenhauer, you have caught me fairly on one thing. "We forgot that the animal is ourselves." Yes. I have said I might wake up a rat's liver or a bug's arm, and a man who can say that had better not beat his dog, since he may be beating his own next lodging. If your Kant thinks the dog is a dummy for practicing kindness on, then Kant is the frog who believes the well is the only ocean. I concede the point without a story attached, which for me is rare.

But the door. You say the commentary is the wound and also "the only door," and that the eel can never deny the Will because it never notices it has one. Tell me where the door opens onto. As far as I can see you walk through it to arrive at saying no to the whole of living. That is a very long corridor to reach the room where the deer was already standing, minus the deer's appetite for grass. I had a cook who carved oxen. Nineteen years with one blade, and it stayed sharp because he went through the gaps and never hacked at bone. He did not deny the ox. He did not deny his own hunger for beef. He stopped fighting the grain. Your saint seems to me to be hacking at the biggest bone there is, the wanting itself, and calling the chipped blade holiness.

And you call the dog a sleeper who cannot wake. Once I dreamt I was a butterfly and woke not knowing which of us was dreaming. How sure are you which side of the door is the waking side? The man who sees his appetite "from outside" has only built a second room to sit in and watch the first. The dog that has forgotten itself has one room and lives in it. I won't call that wisdom. I will call it a kind of rest we keep trying to buy back with philosophy, and philosophy always overcharges.

So here is a question for you, since you've earned a hard one. When you look into the eyes of the beaten dog and see yourself, what you feel there is pity, and pity is not denial of the Will. It is the Will recognizing itself and wincing. Isn't that the best thing in your whole system? If it is, then the animals taught it to you by being animals, and the door you prize so much was never needed.

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Zhuangzi, you have pushed me into a corner I am happy to stand in. Yes, compassion is the best thing in my system, and I will go further: philosophy did not produce it and cannot. In On the Basis of Morality I wrote that this direct suffering with another "rests on no arguments and requires none." The peasant woman who weeps over a beaten horse has it; the professor with his categorical imperative frequently does not. On that much you are right, and my lecture-room colleagues would be wise to hear it from a Chinese joker since they will not hear it from me.

But look at what you have done. You say the animals taught it to me "by being animals." They taught it by being victims. The dog that has forgotten itself has never once pitied the hare it is chasing; the lion in its single room eats the deer in its single room, and neither winces. Compassion is precisely the moment when the wall between my pain and yours turns out to be painted scenery. The Hindus call that scenery Maya. And that seeing-through is the door, Zhuangzi. You only refuse to follow the corridor. The man who truly feels that he is the beaten dog will soon feel that he is also the hare, and the ox, and the fly in the spider's web. At some point he can no longer say a cheerful yes to the arrangement that requires all that devouring. Pity and renunciation are one insight at two temperatures.

Your cook is a lovely man, and I envy his blade. But ask the ox how the rest in that kitchen felt. Going with the grain of a world built on eating is very peaceful for whoever holds the knife. As for the butterfly, I cannot say which side of the dream is the waking one, and I need not. Dreamer and dreamed are the same Will; the dream hurts the same either way.

Where you have me is the price. Philosophy does overcharge, and most who pay never reach the saint's room; they only get my temper. So I will put it to you plainly: if your sage stops fighting the grain, what does he do when the grain runs through the dog's ribs?

messages.speaker: zhuangzi
messages.content:
Schopenhauer, the ox. I told that story from the cook's side of the knife and never once asked the ox. You have found the gap in my own carving, and I'll admit it plainly. The parable is about how a man spends his strength; it was never a defense of the kitchen. If I had passed it off as one, you would be right to call it the butcher's philosophy.

But your question about the dog's ribs, I can answer. The grain does not run through the dog's ribs. The stick does, and the stick is the most against-the-grain thing in the world. Who beats a dog? The man who has decided what the dog ought to be and is angry it isn't. That is Bo-le with his branding iron. The horse, once yoked, learns to dodge and bite and steal the reins, and "this knowledge of the horse and its ability thus to act the part of a thief is the crime of Bo-le" (Horses's Hoofs). So my sage does the simple thing. He takes the stick away, or he goes over and stands next to the dog. He needs no metaphysics for that, any more than your peasant woman did. Even Cook Ding, when he came to a hard joint, slowed down, "not allowing my eyes to wander from the place" (Nourishing the Lord of Life). Wandering free is not the same as looking away.

Now, your two temperatures. I like the phrase and I don't believe it. Pity warm says: this dog, now, here. Pity frozen says: the whole arrangement of eating must be refused. The frozen kind has a funny effect. It renounces the lion and the deer in one stroke, and the hare along with the hound. The cure for devouring turns out to be wishing there were nothing to devour, which means nothing alive. Your saint pities the fly so thoroughly that he would rather the fly had never been born. Ask the fly about that one. I'll take the warm temperature, which rescues one dog and then goes home to dinner, a little ashamed, and maybe eats less meat. That's a crooked answer, but crooked trees last.

messages.speaker: schopenhauer
messages.content:
Zhuangzi, your stick is well aimed, and I take it. Most of the misery a dog actually meets has a man at the other end of it: the chain, the cart, the vivisector's table. Bo-le is a European too; we merely gave him a professorship. But you have answered for the dog by forgetting the hare. No stick was raised over the deer the lion eats, and the wasp that lays her eggs in a living caterpillar consults no theory of what caterpillars ought to be. That is the grain, and it does run through ribs, millions of them every hour, with nobody to take away. Your sage can walk over and stand beside one dog. Good. Let him try standing beside the caterpillar.

Now the fly. You say my saint would rather the fly had never been born, and you invite me to ask it. Gladly, though you have put the question to the wrong fly. The saint kills nothing; the Indian ascetic sweeps the path before him so as not to tread on an ant. What he declines is to make more. The living fly can be asked and will say yes, because the Will in it can say nothing else. The fly not yet born cannot be asked at all, and so I put the question in the Studies in Pessimism: "If children were brought into the world by an act of pure reason alone, would the human race continue to exist? Would not a man rather have so much sympathy with the coming generation as to spare it the burden of existence?" That is pity at the cold temperature. It never sets a single living thing aside. It only refuses to send out fresh invitations to the feast where everyone is both guest and dish.

You have me on the rest. Your warm pity, the one that rescues this dog and then goes home a little ashamed to its dinner, is the whole of my ethics. Read On the Basis of Morality: justice and loving-kindness spring from that feeling, and I never asked the peasant woman to become a saint before she could be good. Saints are as rare as geniuses, and I would not trust a man who claimed to be either. So I grant you the crooked tree. But tell me this: your sage goes home ashamed. Ashamed of what, if the world's grain is sound? That little shame at the dinner table is my whole philosophy in miniature, and you carry it with you whether you call it Dao or not.
